metrics in Amazon CloudWatch. Enable model invocation logging when you need individual request records, then query them with Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights. For the Amazon Bedrock Mantle endpoint, record the response usage fields in your application logs. Its Amazon CloudWatch namespace currently has no separate cache counters.

To check costs, filter AWS Cost Explorer to Amazon Bedrock and group by Usage type. Cache reads, cache writes, and uncached input appear as separate entries per model. Exclude output-token entries when calculating their shares of input cost.

A short checklist

  • Keep the reusable prefix stable. Put shared tools and instructions first, then append conversation history and new turns. Changing a timestamp, message, or tool definition prevents reuse beyond that change. A shorter prefix can still be reused if it has its own saved endpoint.
  • Choose boundaries around content you want to reuse. Use implicit caching for growing history, explicit markers for shared prefixes, or both. Explicit-only mode avoids writing disposable suffixes. When extending an explicit-only conversation, retain earlier markers so later requests can find the saved prefixes.
  • Keep the initial tool catalog unchanged. Use 
    allowed_tools
    to restrict which tools are callable. Append known definitions with 
    additional_tools
    , or discover them through namespaced client-side 
    tool_search
    . Choose a stable tool profile when different agent roles need different catalogs.
  • Check prefix size and lifetime. A cacheable prefix must contain at least 1,024 tokens. Cached prefixes remain eligible for reuse for at least 30 minutes after their latest write or successful reuse.
  • Warm shared content before launching helpers. Mark the shared prefix in both the warm-up and helper requests, including when using implicit mode. Finish the warm-up request before starting parallel calls.
  • Keep cache keys stable within each sharing group. Requests intended to reuse a prefix must use the same key. Separate keys can keep cache accounting distinct between customers or users.
  • Measure savings across the workflow. Cache writes cost 1.25 times the normal input rate. Read prices depend on the model. Track write costs alongside read savings, using response usage during development and monitoring and billing data in production.

Waking up on February 3rd

Bill Murray only escapes Groundhog Day once he stops repeating the same mistakes and starts carrying what he learned from one day to the next. Agents get there in a similar, if less romantic, way: by keeping the start of their prompt byte-for-byte stable and using automatic or explicit cache boundaries as the history grows.

In this post, we covered how to cache shared tools and instructions, grow the cache across agent turns, and preserve reuse when adding tools, launching helpers, or starting new sessions. Keep the shared prefix stable and append new information as the workflow progresses. Use implicit caching for growing conversations and explicit breakpoints for shared content. Combine them when you need both, or choose explicit-only mode when a changing suffix is unlikely to be reused. Compare cache reads, writes, total input cost, and latency to find what works best for your agent. To apply these patterns, follow the Amazon Bedrock prompt caching documentation for OpenAI models and check model availability by AWS Region and endpoint. Start with one workflow and measure the savings as your conversations grow.

entries.title: Build agentic retrieval on a Managed Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base with CDK
entries.summary: Build enterprise agentic retrieval on a Managed Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base with the AWS CDK: an agent that routes across two knowledge bases, retrieves through the AgentCore Gateway, and returns grounded, cited answers, with seven layers of observability and both on-demand and continuous evaluation, all deployed as a single CDK application.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Build agentic retrieval on a Managed Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base with CDK

This post builds enterprise agentic retrieval on a Managed Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base with the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK). To see why that’s worth building, it helps to start with where ordinary Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) breaks down. Most RAG systems start the same way: they embed the question, fetch the nearest chunks from one index, hand them to a model, and return the answer. One retrieval, one generation. For a large class of questions that’s the right design, and there’s no reason to build anything more complicated.

It fails in a recognizable way. Ask a question whose answer spans two corpora, and a single retrieval returns half of what the model needs, which is worse than returning nothing, because the answer comes back fluent and incomplete. Ask a question where the right source depends on the question, and a single index has no mechanism to choose. Ask a question that needs a second look at the corpus after seeing the first result, and there is nowhere for that second look to happen.

Enterprise agentic retrieval answers all three by putting a reasoning agent in the loop. The agent decides whether to retrieve, which knowledge base to consult, and whether to go back for more before it composes an answer. This is the direction Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases have evolved. With the launch of the Managed Knowledge Base, retrieval is no longer a single embed-and-fetch call. It has become an agentic capability: multi-turn planning, tool-driven retrieval, and grounded, cited answers. The AgenticRetrieveStream API offers this as a first-class service feature rather than something you assemble yourself. That works, and it also introduces a genuinely harder operational problem. A single-shot pipeline is a function you can reason about by reading it. An agent that reasons and retrieves in a loop takes a different path on every question. By default you can see neither the path it took nor whether the answer it produced was any good. Observability stops being a nice-to-have and becomes the only way to know the system works.

In August 2024, Build an end-to-end RAG solution using Knowledge Bases for Amazon Bedrock and the AWS CDK deployed the single-shot design as a CDK application: an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) corpus, an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless collection and index, a knowledge base, and a data source, provisioned as CDK stacks whose order you sequenced by hand. Three things have changed since it was published.

  • Amazon Bedrock now offers a managed knowledge base (Type: MANAGED), which owns the ingestion, storage, indexing, and retrieval itself. The OpenSearch Serverless collection and index that post provisions are no longer something you need to create, scale, or pay for with OpenSearch Compute Units (OCUs).
  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides the agentic half, a Gateway that exposes each knowledge base as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool, a Runtime that hosts the reasoning agent, and AgenticRetrieveStream, which reranks internally and returns a synthesized, cited answer. Agentic retrieval is available only on the Managed Knowledge Base.
  • The observability and evaluation story is now something you can provision, not something you bolt on. This solution ships two Amazon CloudWatch dashboards spanning seven layers of telemetry, plus two forms of evaluation, on-demand and continuous, from the same deployment.

This post builds that system: an agent that routes across two knowledge bases, retrieves through the Gateway, and returns a grounded, cited answer, with every layer of its behavior instrumented, as a single AWS CDK application in Python. One command deploys all of it, and CDK derives the order.

If you read the 2024 post, the path from an Amazon S3 bucket to the knowledge base will look familiar, and everything after it is new: the vector store is gone, the retrieval is agentic, and roughly half of what the app provisions exists to tell you what the agent did. If you didn’t, this post stands on its own.

The services at play and the path one question takes through them: the agent decides whether to retrieve and which knowledge base to consult, the Gateway exposes each knowledge base as a tool it can call, the Managed Knowledge Bases search and cite, and the loop repeats as many times as the question needs. Everything the agent does along the way lands in Amazon CloudWatch.

Background

Before the walkthrough, it helps to establish three things: what makes retrieval agentic, why the Managed Knowledge Base is the right foundation for it, and why observability and evaluation belong in the design rather than bolted on later.

From RAG to enterprise agentic retrieval

Classic Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) does one retrieval and one generation. Enterprise agentic retrieval puts a reasoning agent in the loop: it decides whether and what to retrieve, can retrieve several times to refine, chooses which knowledge base is relevant (semantic routing), and only then composes a grounded answer with citations. With the Managed Knowledge Base, this is a first-class service capability, the AgenticRetrieveStream API performs the multi-turn planning, executes the retrieval, and returns a cited answer, rather than an orchestration layer you build and maintain over a raw vector search. That produces better answers on complex questions, but it also produces a more complex system to operate, which is exactly why observability and evaluation are built in from the start.

Managed compared to do-it-yourself Knowledge Bases

Amazon Bedrock now offers a Managed Knowledge Base (Type: MANAGED): Amazon Bedrock manages the ingestion, storage, indexing, and retrieval for you, including embedding and reranking with service-managed models by default, so there is no vector database to provision, scale, or patch. This differs from a Customer-managed (DIY) Knowledge Base, where you choose and operate the vector store (for example, Amazon OpenSearch Serverless) yourself.

Two differences matter most for this solution:

CapabilityAmazon Bedrock managedCustomer-managed (DIY)
Agentic retrieval (AgenticRetrieveStream)✅ Supported❌ Not supported
AgentCore Gateway integration✅ Supported❌ Not supported
Data storeAuto scaling, fully managed by Amazon BedrockYou provision, scale, and maintain it
Embedding + rerankingBuilt-in managed models, no extra costYou configure them
Infrastructure to manageNoneVector DB + more

Because agentic retrieval and the AgentCore Gateway connector are available only on the managed knowledge base, it is the natural foundation for enterprise agentic retrieval. It also means Amazon Bedrock manages the storage and indexing for you, so there is no OpenSearch Serverless collection or OCU capacity to provision in this design. The customer-managed option remains the right choice when you want to select and operate your own vector store, for example to reuse an existing OpenSearch Serverless collection or to meet specific data-residency, tuning, or compliance requirements. For enterprise agentic retrieval, the managed knowledge base is what makes the capability possible.

Why observability and evaluation

An agentic system that returns an answer isn’t enough for production. You need to see how it behaves (latency, call volume, token usage), how good the retrieval and answers are, and you need those signals continuously. This solution ships two CloudWatch dashboards spanning seven layers of telemetry, plus two forms of evaluation (on-demand and continuous), all provisioned by the same CDK application. The grounding, citations, and evaluation layers also support responsible use. Cited answers trace back to their source passages so responses stay auditable, and the faithfulness and correctness scores let you catch answers drifting from their sources rather than finding out in production.

Why CDK for this particular solution

Any infrastructure-as-code tool can create these resources. CDK earns its place here for a reason specific to this architecture: the four stacks are densely cross-referenced. The Gateway needs both knowledge base ids. The agent needs the URL and ARN for the Gateway. The dashboards need the KB ids, the Gateway ARN, and the agent runtime id, seven values crossing stack boundaries, each one a dimension on a metric or a target on a connector.

Written as raw templates, that is a set of stack exports and cross-stack lookups kept in agreement by hand, plus a script that deploys in the right order and threads outputs forward, and both drift the moment anything is renamed. In CDK you pass the construct, and the export and the dependency edge are derived from that one act of passing it. The 2024 solution had three stacks and a mostly linear dependency chain. At four stacks with seven values crossing between them, the difference stops being stylistic.

Solution overview

Here is the path a single question takes through the system, end to end. It’s worth a slow look, because the rest of the post walks through it left to right.

The following diagram traces the end-to-end agentic retrieval workflow. A user’s question enters the agent on the AgentCore Runtime, which routes it through the AgentCore Gateway to one of two AgenticRetrieveStream tools, one per managed knowledge base, financial and weather, each ingested from Amazon S3. The selected tool returns a grounded, cited answer, and every step streams to Amazon CloudWatch and AWS X-Ray. The numbered badges map to the following walkthrough.

The numbered steps in the diagram map to the workflow, which is as follows.

Step 0 — one-time, at deploy. Before any question is asked, each corpus in Amazon S3 is ingested into its own Managed Knowledge Base: Amazon Bedrock parses, chunks, embeds, and indexes it automatically. This happens once when the stacks deploy, it isn’t part of the per-question path, so it is drawn as a dashed arrow and marked step 0. Every question then follows steps 1–6:

  • A user sends a question to the agent hosted on the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime. The Runtime auto-instruments the whole reason-and-act loop with OpenTelemetry (OTEL) spans, so the system is observable from the very first call.
  • The agent’s reasoning model plans and routes across knowledge bases. Because each knowledge base is exposed as its own retrieval tool, the agent selects the tool whose topic matches the question, financial or weather, rather than searching one blended index.
  • The selected tool call is brokered by the AgentCore Gateway over MCP, authorized by the agent’s IAM task role and signed with SigV4, which invokes that knowledge base’s AgenticRetrieveStream API on the Managed Knowledge Base.
  • AgenticRetrieveStream does the within-knowledge-base work: it decomposes the question into sub-queries, retrieves iteratively from the data store that Amazon Bedrock manages (ingested from the corpora in Amazon S3), and synthesizes a grounded, cited answer that streams back through the Gateway.
  • The agent checks whether the returned context is sufficient. If not, it loops, routing and retrieving again, before composing its final answer. If so, it returns the cited answer to the user.
  • Throughout, the Runtime emits spans, token counts, and metrics to Amazon CloudWatch and AWS X-Ray, populating the seven observability layers and feeding both the on-demand and continuous evaluation scores.

Internally, that workflow is one CDK app, 

app.py
, that declares four stacks. You don’t choose the order, CDK derives it from the construct references you pass:

That is the whole wiring. Those four constructor calls are what replace the export/import bookkeeping and the deploy script.

#StackWhat it createsNote
1-kbS3 bucket, corpora upload, two Type: MANAGED KBs, data sources, IAM, ingestionKBs reach ACTIVE, corpora ingested
2-gatewayGateway (AWS_IAM / MCP), per-KB AgenticRetrieveStream targetsno Cognito needed
3-agentECR, CodeBuild, instrumented Strands agent on Runtime, vended logs/traces, online eval~8–10 min (image build)
4-dashboardsagentic-observability + kb-observability dashboardsempty until you drive traffic

The agent runs a reason-and-act loop: it thinks (a large language model (LLM) call), decides which KB tool to call, reads what came back through the Gateway, and often retrieves again before composing its final, cited answer. Every step is auto-instrumented by the Runtime, so the seven observability layers fill from real traffic.

The seven layers. L1 KB-native metrics, L2 ingestion, L3 agentic retrieval quality, L4 Gateway/MCP metrics, L5 OTEL span tree , L6 token usage, and L7 evaluation scores. Layers 1, 4, and 5 are emitted automatically. Layers 3, 6, and 7 are published as custom metrics by the driver notebook.

Everything tunable lives in one file, 

config.py
:
SettingMeaningDefault
EnvSettings.PROJECT_NAME
 Name prefix for every stack and resource
bmkb-obs-cdk
 
EnvSettings.ACCOUNT_REGION
 AWS Region to deploy intous-west-2 (or your profile’s)
KbConfig.EMBEDDING_MODEL_TYPE
 
MANAGED
(bundled) or 
CUSTOM
(bring your own ARN)		 
MANAGED
 
AgentConfig.MODEL_ID
 The agent’s reasoning model, the Layer 6 spendClaude Haiku 4.5
EvalConfig.SAMPLING_PERCENTAGE
 Online-evaluation sampling rate, see the disclaimer100

Changing 

PROJECT_NAME
gives you an independently-named copy of the whole solution, so two deployments can coexist in one account. The driver notebook reads the same constant, so it follows the rename automatically, there are no stack names to keep in sync by hand.

Describe the dataset

The solution ships with two small corpora, bundled in the repository under data/:

  • Financial — A synthetic Octank Financial 10-K (octank_financial_10K.pdf, ~198 KB).
  • Weather — A real, publicly available U.S. Congressional Research Service report on tornadoes (IF12695, tornadoes_report.pdf, ~560 KB).

⚠️ About the data: The financial corpus is synthetic. Octank is a fictional company and the 10-K is model-generated sample data (CC0-licensed). It isn’t real financial data. The weather corpus is a real, public-domain U.S. Government work and is a Congressional Research Service report, publicly available at sgp.fas.org/crs/misc/IF12695.pdf (works of the U.S. Government aren’t subject to copyright). To use your own data, drop files under data/ and adjust the prefixes in 

config.py
, no other change is required.

The two corpora are intentionally distinct, so the agent must route each question to the right knowledge base, the semantic-routing story. Because these are Managed Knowledge Bases, we don’t configure chunking, embedding, or an index: on ingestion, Amazon Bedrock parses each PDF, chunks it, embeds it with its managed model, and indexes it automatically.

We use two separate knowledge bases, each exposed through the Gateway as its own retrieval tool, rather than one knowledge base holding both corpora and that choice is deliberate. Giving the agent two named tools makes routing an explicit act of reasoning it can be observed making: the span tree shows which tool it chose for a given question, and the retrieval-quality metrics in Layer 3 stay separable per knowledge base, so financial and weather precision never blur into a single number. A single tool spanning both corpora would collapse that distinction, the routing decision would move inside one index’s ranking, out of view, and every quality signal would be an average across two unrelated domains. Keeping the corpora and their tools separate is what makes the agent’s behavior legible, which is the whole point of the exercise.

In CDK, getting the corpora into S3 is a BucketDeployment:

BucketDeployment is worth knowing about precisely because the alternative is so tempting: without it, the custom resource that triggers ingestion tends to grow an upload step, and now one resource owns two unrelated jobs. Here it only has to ingest.

Managed ingestion scans, chunks, embeds, and indexes each document automatically: one document indexed per knowledge base, zero failures.

Deploy the solution

This section walks through deploying the whole solution with one command. After the prerequisites are met, 

cdk deploy --all
provisions all four stacks in CDK’s derived dependency order and threads every cross-stack value through automatically.

Prerequisites

  • An AWS account with permissions for Amazon Bedrock, AgentCore (Runtime + Gateway), AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), CloudWatch, AWS X-Ray, Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR), AWS CodeBuild, Amazon S3, AWS Lambda, and AWS CloudFormation.
  • The agent’s model available in the account (default 
    us.anthropic.claude-haiku-4-5-20251001-v1:0
    ).
  • CloudWatch Transaction Search enabled, so OTEL spans land in aws/spans for Layers 5–7.
  • Node.js 18+ and the CDK CLI (
    npm install -g aws-cdk
    ), plus Python 3.13+.
  • The account and region bootstrapped for CDK (cdk bootstrap), once per account/region.
  • No local Docker, the agent image is built by CodeBuild (ARM64).

One command

To deploy the solution, clone the repository, create a virtual environment, install the dependencies, and run 

cdk deploy --all
. Run the following commands from your terminal:

The first two commands clone the sample and move into the project directory. The next two create and activate a Python virtual environment and install the CDK app’s dependencies. 

cdk bootstrap
prepares the account and region for CDK (you only need it once per account/region), and 
cdk deploy --all
provisions all four stacks.

Account and region come from your AWS profile (CDK_DEFAULT_ACCOUNT / CDK_DEFAULT_REGION), so the app deploys with no edits.

Region availability: The managed knowledge base, agentic retrieval (AgenticRetrieveStream), and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (Runtime and Gateway) aren’t available in every AWS Region. Before you deploy, confirm that all of these are offered in your target Region, and set 

ACCOUNT_REGION
in 
config.py
accordingly. The default is us-west-2. For current availability, see the Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation and the AWS Regional Services List.

There is no deploy script in this version, and that is the point: 

cdk deploy --all
walks the dependency graph it derived from 
app.py
, deploys the four stacks in order, and passes every cross-stack value automatically. The terminal reports each stack as it completes, bmkb-obs-cdk-kb [1/4] (the default PROJECT_NAME), then gateway [2/4], then agent [3/4], then dashboards [4/4] and that order is derived, not declared: it falls out of the construct references between the stacks, so adding a fifth stack that consumes an existing output reorders the deploy on its own.

Stack -agent builds the agent container with CodeBuild, so allow roughly 8–10 minutes for that stage. The other three are quick. Each stack prints its outputs on completion, which is where you pick up the knowledge base ids, the Gateway URL, the runtime ARN, and both dashboard URLs. When the deploy finishes, all four stacks are complete. The following screenshot shows the AWS CloudFormation console after a successful 

cdk deploy --all
.

On the console, all four stacks, kb, gateway, agent, and dashboards, report CREATE_COMPLETE, each with its [n/4] position in the derived dependency order shown in its description.

A note on long-running resources

Two things in this solution take far longer than the 15-minute ceiling of an AWS Lambda function allows for naive polling: the KB ingestion sync and the CodeBuild image build. The AWS CDK Provider framework handles this with an 

on_event
/ 
is_complete
split, where one handler starts the work and a second is polled until it reports done.

Nothing blocks, the response protocol back to CloudFormation is owned by the framework rather than hand-written into each handler, and the 30-minute budget is a property rather than something to engineer around.

Launch and test

Open notebooks/01-drive-and-observe.ipynb and run it top to bottom (

pip install -r requirements-notebook.txt
first). It reads the stack outputs, then sends topic-specific prompts to the deployed agent, one session per KB, so you can see both the answers and the semantic routing in one place: financial questions are answered from the Octank 10-K and weather questions from the tornadoes report, each routed to the matching AgenticRetrieveStream tool automatically.

The notebook discovers everything from the stack outputs, so there is nothing to paste in by hand:

The notebook imports the same 

config.py
the app does, so the two can never disagree about what the stacks are called.

The driver sends per-KB prompts through the deployed agent. Financial questions route to the financial KB and weather questions to the weather KB, each with a grounded, cited answer.

The notebook also computes the reference-free Layer 3 retrieval-quality signals from what the agent actually retrieved and cited, no ground truth, no extra judge, and publishes them to CloudWatch.

Observe: The seven-layer dashboards

The two dashboards are where the seven layers become visible. The stack creates both dashboards, and driving traffic populates them. The following screenshot shows the two dashboards as they appear in the CloudWatch console.

Both dashboards appear in the CloudWatch console: one for end-to-end agentic observability and one for per-KB observability (BMKB, Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base). The rest of this section walks through what each layer shows.

In this version the dashboards are built from typed objects rather than a JSON string. A metric is a Metric, a widget is a GraphWidget, and the layout is a list of Rows:

The practical benefit isn’t fewer lines, 

dashboards_stack.py
runs to 400 lines, more than the equivalent DashboardBody JSON would. It is that a misspelled property or an invalid widget combination fails at 
cdk synth
, on your laptop, in about a second. The same mistake inside a DashboardBody string deploys successfully and renders as a broken widget on the AWS Management Console, where you find it by looking at it.

Because a Row accepts any widget, the documentation is part of the layout rather than a wiki page that drifts. Each dashboard interleaves TextWidgets with the graphs:

_l3_explainer() returns a markdown table defining each ratio and how to read it, so the widget that explains grounded_coverage ships in the same commit as the widget that plots it, and a reader who opens the dashboard cold doesn’t need to guess what a reference-free metric is.

Dashboard A — agentic observability (end to end). The board opens with an explainer of how each layer counts a different thing (for N queries you’ll see ~N agent invocations, ~2N retrievals, ~3N LLM calls, and ~5N Gateway MCP operations, the agentic loop made visible), then shows KB metrics (L1), Gateway metrics and latency (L4), token usage (L6), and because the agent uses AgenticRetrieveStream, which returns a synthesized, cited answer rather than per-chunk scores, the reference-free Layer 3 quality signals, defined inline and plotted per KB.

On Dashboard A, the Layer 3 reference-free quality signals are plotted per knowledge base. First, the financial KB. The following chart plots its retrieval_utilization, grounded_coverage, and duplicate_rate.

The weather KB shows the same three signals, tracked separately so the two domains never blur into one number.

The two charts plot retrieval_utilization, grounded_coverage, and duplicate_rate for the financial KB (left) and the weather KB (right), so each knowledge base’s retrieval quality stays separable rather than averaged into one number.

Dashboard B — per-KB (BMKB) observability. The operational signals that also determine spend, per KB: index size (from S3 source bytes), retrieve volume, agentic tool-calls, session token usage, and generation token usage by model, each with an inline explanation.

The following screenshots show Dashboard B’s four metric widgets, populated after a run. The first widget reports index size, derived from S3 source bytes, per knowledge base.

The second widget counts retrieve calls per knowledge base.

The third widget counts agentic tool-calls through the Gateway. This one is shared across both KBs rather than split.

The fourth widget reports session token usage per knowledge base.

The four widgets show index size (from S3 source bytes), retrieve-call volume, agentic tool-calls through the Gateway, and session token usage. Each is broken out per knowledge base except the Gateway tool-call count, which is shared across both.

One dimension detail is worth calling out, because the typed API won’t catch it for you: the 

AWS/Bedrock/KnowledgeBases
namespace expects a prefixed id, 
knowledge-base/
, while the solution’s own 
BMKB/*
namespaces use the bare id. Both are only strings as far as CDK is concerned.

Layer 5: The span tree

Layer 5 is the raw OTEL span tree in aws/spans, and it is the layer that shows you the agentic loop directly. It is worth reading carefully, because the nesting isn’t obvious: one LLM call produces three spans. The Strands 

invoke_agent
span wraps the turn, an internal 
chat
span wraps the model call, and a 
chat
span of kind 
CLIENT
is the actual call, and all three repeat the same 
gen_ai.usage.*
token attributes.

The following screenshot shows the span tree in aws/spans, with the three-span nesting visible in the top rows.

Reading the top three rows: an invoke_agent Strands Agents aggregate, then an internal chat span, then a CLIENT chat span, all reporting an identical 7,299 input and 268 output tokens. That is the same LLM call appearing at three levels of the tree, which is why aggregation needs care.

That structure matters the moment you aggregate. To count each LLM call once, filter to the 

CLIENT
leaf:

Without that filter the same query reports three times the tokens and three times the calls.

Applying that CLIENT-leaf filter, the following screenshot shows generation token usage by model with each LLM call counted once.

With the filter in place, the run shows 14 LLM calls totaling 60,472 input and 2,709 output tokens. Without it, the same query would report three times the calls and three times the tokens.

Evaluate: On-demand and continuous

Quality is measured two ways, and both are provisioned by the app.

On-demand: The driver notebook calls AgentCore There is no deploy script in this version, and that is the point: (LLM-as-judge) over each session’s spans for built-in evaluators, Correctness, Faithfulness, Tool-Selection Accuracy and publishes the scores to CloudWatch, where they appear as Layer 7 on Dashboard A.

The following screenshot shows Layer 7 on Dashboard A: on-demand evaluation scores per knowledge base, with the Layer 5 OTEL span table on the same dashboard.

Layer 7 shows the on-demand evaluation scores per knowledge base, with the Layer 5 OTEL span table alongside, so the scores and the spans that produced them read together on one board.

Continuous (online): The agent stack also provisions an 

AWS::BedrockAgentCore::OnlineEvaluationConfig
that samples live sessions and scores them automatically, no notebook run required. The configuration itself is visible in the Bedrock AgentCore console under Assess → Evaluations → Evaluation configurations. Results land in the log group 
/aws/bedrock-agentcore/evaluations/results/
, and every score is also published as a CloudWatch metric in the 
Bedrock-AgentCore/Evaluations
namespace, keyed by evaluator name and configuration id, so you can graph the scores or alarm on them without parsing logs.

The following screenshot shows the online evaluation configuration in the AgentCore console, under Assess, then Evaluations, then Evaluation configurations.

The configuration lists four built-in evaluators, Tool-Selection Accuracy, Faithfulness, Correctness, and Response Relevance, set to 100 percent sampling and shown as ACTIVE and enabled.

Because the scores are ordinary CloudWatch metrics, they graph like anything else, no log parsing, and the same widget could carry an alarm. The following screenshot shows those four evaluator scores graphed as ordinary CloudWatch metrics.

The four evaluator scores appear as metrics in the 

Bedrock-AgentCore/Evaluations
namespace, each keyed to the evaluation configuration id and the agent’s service name, so you can graph them or alarm on them without parsing logs.

Online results only arrive after a session closes. Scoring runs on the completed session, so the results log group stays empty for roughly the session idle timeout (~30 minutes) after you drive traffic. An empty group right after a run is expected, not a misconfiguration. Each result event carries 

session.id
, so it joins to every other layer. The on-demand path in the notebook has no such wait, which is why both are here.

Across the four built-in evaluators on this run, the continuous path scored 1.00 on Correctness, Faithfulness, Response Relevance, and Tool-Selection Accuracy, five scored traces per evaluator, each result carrying a written explanation.

⚠️ Sampling and cost. This app sets SAMPLING_PERCENTAGE = 100 purely for the blog experiment, so every session is scored and the results are immediately visible. This isn’t a production recommendation. Online evaluation invokes an LLM-as-judge per sampled session, so cost scales with the sampling rate and traffic volume. For a real deployment, choose a sampling percentage that fits your quality-monitoring needs and budget, and align the configuration with your organization’s own policies and cost-governance requirements before enabling it. The rate is a single constant, 

EvalConfig.SAMPLING_PERCENTAGE
, in 
config.py
.

Clean up

When you’re finished, remove the solution so it stops incurring charges, since stored KB data, the agent image in ECR, and the still-active online evaluation all cost money while the stacks sit idle. One command tears everything down:

CDK deletes the stacks in reverse dependency order on its own, dashboards, then agent, then gateway, then kb: the same graph it derived for the deploy, walked backward. There is no teardown script to keep in agreement with the deploy script, which is one of the more quietly valuable properties of modelling the dependencies once.

Two removal behaviors are worth knowing, because both replace hand-written cleanup code:

Both are set for sample hygiene, for anything you care about, switch the bucket to 

RemovalPolicy.RETAIN
.

The CDK bootstrap stack (

CDKToolkit
) and its staging bucket aren’t removed. They are shared account-wide infrastructure that other CDK apps may depend on.

What changed since the single-shot solution

Both this post and the 2024 solution are CDK applications in Python, deployed with 

cdk deploy
. The authoring tool is the constant here, what changed is the architecture underneath it, and most of the change is subtraction:
Concern2024: Single-shot RAGThis solution
Vector storeAn OpenSearch Serverless collection and index you provision, scale, and pay OCU forNone. Type: MANAGED, Amazon Bedrock owns storage and indexing
Index lifecycleA custom resource creates the index and waits for it to become searchableNothing to create
Embedding modelYou select it and grant model accessService-managed by default
Stacks3: KB role → OpenSearch infra → KB + data source4: kb → gateway → agent → dashboards
RetrievalOne Retrieve, top-k chunks by vector similarityAgenticRetrieveStream, reranked internally, returns a synthesized cited answer
Choosing a knowledge baseNot applicable, there is one indexThe agent routes semantically across two
Second look at the corpusNot possible in one shotThe agent retrieves again before answering
TelemetryNone provisionedSeven layers, two dashboards
EvaluationManual: sync, pick a model, ask questionsOn-demand and continuous, both provisioned
Cost floor when idleOCU charges accrue whether or not you queryStorage only

The trade is real in both directions. A single index answering single-shot questions is cheaper per query, simpler to reason about, and entirely sufficient when one corpus holds the answer. Reach for this design when it doesn’t.

The CDK constructs doing the work

Four constructs carry most of the weight in this app, and they are worth naming because each replaces something people otherwise hand-write:

  • Provider – For custom resources that outlive the 15-minute ceiling of an AWS Lambda function. The 
    on_event
    / 
    is_complete
    split means nothing sleeps in a poll loop, and the response protocol back to CloudFormation is the framework’s job rather than a vendored 
    urllib
    callback in every handler.
  • BucketDeployment – Uploads the corpora, so the ingestion custom resource only ingests.
  • auto_delete_objects=True and empty_on_delete=True, replace the hand-written 
    list_object_versions
    and image-delete loops that a stack otherwise needs to be destroyable at all.
  • repository.grant_pull_push(project) – One line for the eight 
    ecr:*
    actions CodeBuild needs, spelled correctly by construction.

And typed dashboards, from the Observe section: Metric / GraphWidget / Row objects instead of a DashboardBody JSON string, which moves an invalid widget combination from “renders broken on the console” to “fails at 

cdk synth
.”

Two things CDK doesn’t change, and both are worth knowing before you start:

  • Free-form JSON stays camelCase. 
    connector_parameters
    and 
    parameter_values
    are passed through verbatim, so the AWS CDK snake_case to PascalCase conversion does not apply inside them. Keys like 
    bucketName
    and 
    inclusionPrefixes
    must be spelled exactly as the API expects, and nothing will tell you otherwise until the resource fails.
  • String-typed values are still strings. The 
    knowledge-base/
    versus bare
    dimension difference from the Observe section is invisible to the type system. Typed constructs check structure, not semantics.

Neither is a reason to prefer one tool over the other. They are the boundary of what “typed” buys you, and knowing where that boundary sits is most of what makes CDK pleasant instead of surprising.

Conclusion

We built a complete enterprise agentic retrieval solution on a Managed Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base and AgentCore: multi-KB semantic routing, a reasoning agent, seven layers of observability, and both on-demand and continuous evaluation, and deployed all of it as a single AWS CDK application.

Two things are worth taking away. The managed knowledge base removed infrastructure rather than adding it: no vector store to provision, no index to create and wait on, no OCU line item accruing while the system sits idle. It is also the knowledge base type that supports agentic retrieval and the AgentCore Gateway connector, as described in the Amazon Bedrock documentation. And once retrieval became agentic, observability stopped being optional. Roughly half of what this app provisions exists to answer what the agent actually did and whether the answer was any good, which isn’t overhead on an agentic system. It’s the part that makes one operable.

The CDK authoring model earned its place on the seams. Seven values cross stack boundaries in this architecture, and every one of them is a construct reference rather than an export/import pair, which is also why there’s no deploy script, no teardown script, and no fixed order to remember.

From here you can point the data sources at your own corpora, place the agent in a virtual private cloud (VPC), tune the online-evaluation sampling rate to your budget and policies, or add more knowledge bases to the router. To learn more, see the Amazon Bedrock detail page and the Amazon Bedrock documentation. The app, the driver notebook, and the self-contained utilities are all in the accompanying GitHub repository, so you can clone it and deploy your own copy with one command.

entries.title: Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning on Amazon SageMaker AI: A hands-on guide
entries.summary: Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning (MTRL) on Amazon SageMaker AI trains models on the outcome of a whole multi-step task rather than labeled steps. This hands-on guide walks the full pipeline using Wordle: deploying the agent and reward on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, preparing the dataset, training, and evaluating at serving settings.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning on Amazon SageMaker AI: A hands-on guide

Most fine-tuning teaches a model to produce a better answer to a single prompt. Agentic tasks are different. An agent that files an expense report or triages a support ticket takes a sequence of actions, and each step depends on what came before. There’s rarely one correct sequence to imitate, and the only reliable feedback is whether the whole sequence succeeded. Supervised fine-tuning has no labels for that, and single-turn reinforcement learning cannot credit a decision made three steps before the outcome.

Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning (MTRL) on Amazon SageMaker AI trains models on exactly that signal. SageMaker AI sends prompts to an agent you host on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, or on your own infrastructure, such as Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2), or AWS Fargate, through an AWS Lambda forwarder. The example here uses AgentCore. The agent calls the policy model being trained, acts in your environment over as many turns as the task needs, and reports one reward when the episode ends. You don’t specify the right trajectory, only how to score the result.

This post uses Wordle, a game in which a player has six tries to guess a hidden five-letter word, as the example. After each guess, every letter turns green if it is in the right position, yellow if it’s in the word but in a different position, and gray if it isn’t in the word. The game suits MTRL because the rules are few, each guess depends on the feedback from the last, and the outcome is scored objectively. Wordle is a teaching example, and frontier models already play it well. In practice, you would use MTRL to make a small, low-cost model good at a multi-step task specific to your business, such as an internal workflow that public models were never trained on. The same pipeline applies to that setting.

In our run, MTRL took gpt-oss-20b from a 61 to an 84 percent solve rate on held-out words at its default reasoning effort, and from 15 to 69 percent at the low effort it trained at, for about $339 in training tokens. In this post, we walk through the pipeline end-to-end: deploying the agent and reward to AgentCore, preparing the dataset, training, monitoring in MLflow, and evaluating at serving settings. We also share the reward-design mistakes and training failures we hit. Your datasets, agent, and trained model stay in your AWS account and are not used to train the base models. All code is in the accompanying aws-samples repository.

Solution overview

The system has two halves. SageMaker AI owns the training job and the policy model. AgentCore hosts the agent, the Wordle environment, and the reward function. The following diagram shows how they connect.

For every rollout, the MTRL service invokes the AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with one training row, which holds one secret word. A Strands agent in the runtime calls the policy model through the SageMaker Job Runtime’s OpenAI-compatible endpoint. The model plays up to six guesses through one tool, 

guess_word
, and after each guess the environment returns per-letter feedback and a summary of what is known. When the game ends, the agent returns one reward. Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) uses the spread of rewards across several rollouts of the same word to update a Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapter on the policy model.

Three design points matter for what follows:

  • The agent and reward live in one place. A single Python file deployed to AgentCore holds the environment, the tool, and the scoring function.
  • The dataset carries only the secret word. The word lists bundled with the agent are built from the open-source SCOWL word lists and are used only for scoring.
  • The reward is outcome-dominant. A solve pays 1.05–1.55 depending on speed, a loss pays -0.5, and never making a valid guess pays -1.5. A small shaping term rewards good strategy within each tier.

Supported models and AWS Regions

MTRL is serverless: you pick a base model and the service provisions the training and sampling infrastructure. At the time of writing, it supports the following base models, each trained with a LoRA adapter:

Base modelAWS Regions
Amazon Nova 2 LiteUS East (N. Virginia) (us-east-1), US West (Oregon) (us-west-2)
GPT-OSS-20B
 US East (N. Virginia) (us-east-1), US West (Oregon) (us-west-2)
Gemma 4 31B (instruction-tuned)US West (Oregon) (us-west-2)
Qwen 3.6 27BUS West (Oregon) (us-west-2)

We chose 

GPT-OSS-20B
because it has the lowest per-token price of the four and its reasoning effort is controllable per request. See the MTRL documentation for the current list.

Pricing

You don’t choose instances or size a cluster. You pay per million tokens in three dimensions, priced by base model:

  • Prefill: input tokens the policy model processes. These accumulate in a multi-turn task, because every turn re-reads the history.
  • Sample: tokens the policy model generates, including reasoning tokens.
  • Train: tokens processed in the backward pass that updates the LoRA adapter.

The 100-step run consumed 491.6 million prefill, 159.7 million sample, and 643.3 million train tokens across 105,486 rollouts in 12 hours 40 minutes. At 

GPT-OSS-20B
list prices in the US East (N. Virginia) Region (us-east-1) at the time of writing, that is about $339:
DimensionTokensPrice per 1MCost
Prefill491,616,806$0.12$58.99
Sample159,737,098$0.30$47.92
Train643,308,554$0.36$231.59
Total1,294,662,458$338.50

The train dimension dominates and scales with trajectory length, so shorter games and less verbose reasoning cut the bill. The AgentCore runtime bills separately for the vCPU and memory the agent uses. For this run, that was about $79, from the runtime’s Amazon CloudWatch usage metrics at us-east-1 list prices. 

DescribeJob
reports the token counts under 
BillableTokenUsage
. See Amazon SageMaker AI pricing for current rates.

Prerequisites

To follow this walkthrough, you need the following. See also the MTRL prerequisites.

  • Python 3.10 or later, uv, Node 20 or later, and the AgentCore CLI (
    npm install -g @aws/agentcore
    ). See Get started with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for installation and the IAM permissions the CLI needs.
  • botocore 1.43.37 or later, on the machine that launches the job. This is the first version that includes the 
    AgentRFT
    CreateJob
    operation.
  • Two AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles, described in Step 1.
  • An Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket in the same Region as the agent. The training job must also run in that Region, because 
    CreateJob
    rejects a cross-Region runtime ARN.

Step 1: Create the IAM roles

MTRL uses two roles, and one of them has a trust policy that the general SageMaker AI documentation doesn’t mention.

Agent runtime role. 

agentcore deploy
creates this role for you. It trusts 
bedrock-agentcore.amazonaws.com
and needs the 
AmazonSageMakerJobRuntimeAccess
managed policy, which lets the agent call the policy model and report rewards. The CDK stack in the sample repository attaches this policy automatically.

Training job role. You create this one. It must trust 

job.sagemaker.amazonaws.com
with both 
sts:AssumeRole
and 
sts:TagSession
, and it needs the 
AmazonSageMakerJobFullAccess
managed policy.

Note: The trust principal is 

job.sagemaker.amazonaws.com
, not 
sagemaker.amazonaws.com
. With the generic principal, 
CreateJob
fails with “Could not assume role,” and the message names the correct principal only after retries.

Step 2: Deploy the agent to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

Clone the sample repository, set your account and Region in Wordle/agentcore/

aws-targets.json
, and deploy:

The CLI builds the agent’s dependencies for the runtime’s Linux ARM64 platform, creates the execution role with 

AmazonSageMakerJobRuntimeAccess
attached, and deploys through AWS CloudFormation. We recommend it over uploading a code package on the console, where it’s common to get the roughly 700 MB of compiled dependencies or the policy attachment wrong. Note the runtime ARN in the output for the training job.

The runtime reads two environment variables from 

agentcore.json
. 
REASONING_EFFORT=low
sets 
reasoning_effort
on every request to the policy model. In our evaluation jobs, low effort used 63 to 83 percent fewer sample tokens per game than medium. 
REASONING_PROMPT_HINT=true
also adds “Reasoning: low” to the system prompt, which is how gpt-oss reads the setting in its Harmony chat format. Neither variable gives the model any hint about the secret word.

The agent is one file, 

main.py
. Simplified, its entrypoint looks like the following. For your own task, you change the task parsing, the tools, and the reward:

Important: The 

sagemaker_rft_handler
decorator does not start an HTTP server by itself. Wrap it with 
BedrockAgentCoreApp
and 
@app.entrypoint
, with the entrypoint decorator outermost. Without this, every invocation times out after 30 seconds.

Step 3: Verify the runtime

Before spending GPU time, confirm the whole chain works with a payload shaped like the one the training service sends. The repository includes one as Wordle/

payload.json
:

The fake job ARN is expected to fail, and the way it fails is the proof. Put your own account ID into it first: for a job ARN in another account, the service returns a 403 before it checks whether the job exists, which looks like a broken IAM setup. From the Wordle directory, run:

In the runtime’s Amazon CloudWatch logs, you see the agent parse the prompt, authenticate to the Job Runtime endpoint, and receive a 400 error reading “Could not find job.” That failure confirms that parsing, authentication, and error reporting work. The command itself prints {“reward”: -1.5}, because the agent never reached the policy model. A 403 reading “not authorized to access this resource” means the job ARN still names another account. A 30-second timeout instead means the HTTP server is not starting (see the Important note in Step 2).

Step 4: Prepare the dataset

The MTRL dataset has no target responses, transcripts, or labels. Each row is one task for the agent to attempt. Here are the first three rows of the training file:

The service reads the 

prompt
column (or the first column) and passes the string to your agent verbatim, without parsing it. We made the string a small JSON object with three fields:
  • prompt: the instruction the agent shows the policy model, identical on every row.
  • answer: the secret word. Only the environment and the reward function use it. The policy model never sees it.
  • id: a row ID for tracing a rollout in the logs back to its source row.

The sample repository’s 

make_dataset.py
draws 640 training words (five full batches of 128) and 128 validation words from the answer list with no overlap, so the validation solve rate measures generalization. The service also accepts Apache Parquet, JSON arrays, and CSV. Upload both files to Amazon S3:

Because the service never inspects the 

prompt
string, a production task can pack a full message list, tool configuration, or reward specification into it. See the MTRL documentation for examples, including how to protect sensitive content in the string.

Step 5: Launch the training job

The launcher uses the 

MultiTurnRLTrainer
class from the 
sagemaker-train
SDK. Point it at the runtime ARN from Step 2, the role from Step 1, the datasets from Step 4, and an MLflow app for metrics. The MLflow app is required, so if you don’t have one, create it first with 
aws sagemaker create-mlflow-app
:

The launcher overrides three hyperparameters and leaves every other one at the gpt-oss-20b default. It sets 

sampling_max_tokens
to 8192, the service maximum, because at the default of 4096 gpt-oss often ran out of tokens while reasoning, before its first tool call. It sets 
max_epochs
to 20 and 
max_steps
to 100: 640 rows at the default 
global_batch_size
of 128 is 5 steps per epoch, and with the default 
group_size
of 8, each step plays 1,024 games. The job moves through Starting, Downloading, and Pending before reaching Training. After it’s training, your AgentCore runtime begins receiving rollout invocations.

Important: Don’t redeploy the agent while a job is running. Redeploying restarts the runtime, in-flight rollouts see no sampling requests, and the service fails the entire job.

Step 6: Monitor training in MLflow

The service logs reward, token, and turn statistics at every step and runs validation every 

val_every
steps. The metric to watch is 
val/reward/pass_at_1
, the fraction of held-out words solved. Every solve scores at least 1.01, so it clears the service’s 
success_threshold
of 1.0 and pass@1 counts it. The following chart is built from this run’s MLflow history:

Training reward climbs to about +0.57 within 15 steps and holds there. Validation reward stays lower, mostly because of temperature 1.0 versus 0 rather than overfitting (see Step 7). The validation solve rate jumps from 2 to 31 percent in the first 10 steps, then moves between 35 and 48 percent. With 128 words, those swings are mostly noise. We did not test whether more steps help at serving settings.

The runtime’s OpenTelemetry traces in CloudWatch record every model turn and tool call. Here is one game the trained model played during an evaluation job (medium effort, temperature 1.0), with the reasoning trimmed. The secret word was PASTE:

A trained-model rollout from the AgentCore runtime traces. The model keeps green letters in place, never reuses a gray letter, and uses each yellow letter to rule out positions, though nothing in the training data showed it how.

Step 7: Evaluate the trained model at serving settings

When the job completes, its page in SageMaker AI Studio shows the status and the model package group that holds the trained model. 

DescribeJob
, with 
JobCategory
set to 
AgentRFT
, returns the output model package ARN and the billable token counts.

An evaluation job (

JobCategory
set to 
AgentRFTEvaluation
) plays your evaluation prompts through the same AgentCore runtime and reward, on the base model or the trained package, and logs 
eval/reward/pass_at_1
to MLflow. Unlike training validation, you can set the temperature. The repository’s launcher runs evaluations back to back, because the default quota allows one evaluation job at a time (you can request an increase):

Each 128-word evaluation took four to seven minutes. Reasoning effort comes from the agent’s environment variables, so to change it you edit 

REASONING_EFFORT
, redeploy, and evaluate. We evaluated both models at low and medium effort and at temperature 0 and 1.0:

The gray segment of each bar is the base model and the blue segment is the gain from training. The low-effort, temperature-0 pair is the training job’s validation at steps 0 and 100. The medium-effort, temperature-1.0 trained result is the mean of two runs (80 and 88 percent).

At temperature 0, both models often end the game without a solve, at either effort. With sampling on, medium effort adds 15 points for the trained model and 46 for the base model. The adapter adds 14–54 points in every setting, so what training taught transfers across settings.

The training job’s own validation curve in MLflow told a different story: it peaked at 48 percent at step 90 and ended at 37 percent, scored at temperature 0. The hyperparameters reference recommends temperature 0 for evaluation because greedy decoding makes curves deterministic and comparable across runs. We report temperature 1.0 because that’s how we serve the model. At medium effort and temperature 1.0, the trained model solves 84 percent of held-out words, up from 61 percent for the base model.

Tip: Evaluate at the settings you will serve at. The training curve says this adapter ends at 37 percent. At serving settings it solves 84 percent. The evaluation jobs that show this cost about $1.20 in tokens and took about an hour.

Step 8: Clean up

Training and evaluation jobs stop billing when they complete, but the AgentCore runtime, its IAM role, the MLflow app, and the S3 objects persist. From the project directory:

Because 

agentcore remove all
rewrites the files under 
agentcore/
, run 
git checkout -- agentcore/
if you want to redeploy later. Deleting the 
AgentCore-Wordle-default
CloudFormation stack removes the same resources and leaves the files alone. The training job role and the model packages are not billed.

Deep dive: Designing the reward

Our reward needed one revision, and the mistake is a common one.

The first design summed the per-guess scoring from the wordle-lora-rl project over the whole game. That scoring works there because each guess is an independent training sample. Summed into one reward per game, it produced two inversions we found only by reading traces:

  • A lost game paid positive reward. Six turns of bonuses added up to about +0.49.
  • Solving on turn 1 scored below solving on turn 3. A first-guess solve earned +0.99 and a third-guess solve earned +1.61, because the extra turns collected more bonuses.

The fix separates a dominant outcome term from a small, bounded shaping term:

The outcome term is set entirely by how the game ended:

OutcomeValue
Solved on guess n1.05 + 0.5 * (6 – n) / 5, so 1.55 on guess 1 down to 1.05 on guess 6
Played all six guesses, unsolved-0.5
Never made a valid guess-1.5

The shaping term is that per-guess scoring, summed over the game:

  • Penalties for contradicting a known green, yellow, or gray letter, for repeating a guess, and for words outside the dictionary.
  • An entropy bonus for a strong opening word.
  • Bonuses for trying new letters and for shrinking the set of remaining possibilities.

The sum is clipped to [-1, 1] and scaled by 0.04 for a solve and 0.15 for a loss, so it separates games with the same outcome but never moves a game into another tier. With typical shaping values:

ScenarioReward
Solve on guess 1+1.550
Solve on guess 3+1.375
Solve on guess 6+1.069
Lost after six guesses-0.427
Never made a valid guess-1.500

A faster solve now always beats a slower one, every solve beats every loss, and never playing is the worst outcome. Our first fix used a single weight of 0.15, which let a guess-3 solve with full shaping (+1.45) outscore a guess-2 solve with the minimum (+1.25). Adjacent guess counts are 0.1 apart, so a smaller solve weight of 0.04 removes the overlap, and the worst solve (+1.01) still clears the 1.0 success threshold. Shaping still matters because GRPO learns from reward variance within a group, so two lost games that differ in clue consistency still teach the model something. As the SageMaker AI documentation advises, start with an outcome-based reward, add shaping sparingly, and check the reward on real trajectories.

Deep dive: What went wrong, in the order you will hit it

Each of these cost at least one training run.

  • Bearer tokens under concurrency. Minting a token with a fresh botocore session per call starved the credential provider at 32 concurrent rollouts, and caching tokens for an hour returned 403 errors as credentials rotated. The fix is one self-refreshing session, a short cache, and a re-sign on 403.
  • A rollout that never reaches the policy model fails the whole job. When every model call in a rollout failed authentication, the service ended the job with “No sampling requests were received.” Returning an error status fails it too, so always return a reward. A game where the model is sampled but never makes a valid guess is fine: it scores -1.5, and the 100-step run had 51 of them in about 105,000 rollouts.
  • Tool calls drift into plain text. At too high a learning rate, the model wrote tool calls as text, every rollout got the same floor reward, and the gradient vanished. The agent now recovers guesses from raw text with a small formatting penalty.
  • The plateau. Training reward stopped rising after about step 15 and validation stopped improving after about step 30, though at temperature 0 validation understates the model (Step 7). A curriculum that seeds games with prior guesses, or more rollouts per word than the default 
    group_size
    of 8, is what we would try next.

Conclusion

MTRL on SageMaker AI trains a model on the outcome of a whole episode. That fits agentic tasks, where the right trajectory is unknown and only the result can be scored. We used a single episode-level reward. When intermediate steps can be scored too, MTRL also accepts one reward per turn through the UpdateReward API. In this post, an open-weight 20B model reached an 84 percent solve rate at serving settings, up from 61 percent, for about $339 in training tokens and about $79 in AgentCore runtime usage. The 37 percent the training curve reports is an artifact of how the training job scores validation, so evaluate at the settings you will serve at.

The same pipeline applies to internal procedures, tools, and workflows that public models were never trained on.

To get started, clone the sample repository, follow the preceding steps, and run the smoke test in Step 3 before committing GPU time. For the underlying APIs, see the SageMaker AI MTRL documentation.

entries.title: Orchestrating SageMaker AI endpoint auto scaling with AWS CDK
entries.summary: Updating a SageMaker AI endpoint that has Application Auto Scaling registered makes AWS CloudFormation and AWS CDK deployments fail. This post shows how to build a reusable AWS CDK construct with CloudFormation custom resources that deregisters and re-registers auto scaling automatically, so you can update the endpoint and its scaling in a single deployment.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Orchestrating SageMaker AI endpoint auto scaling with AWS CDK

Updating the Amazon Sagemaker AI real-time endpoint configuration (changing the instance type, instance count, or environment variables) causes deployments through AWS CloudFormation or the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) to fail. SageMaker AI requires you to deregister the scalable target before updating the endpoint, but when you deregister it, CloudFormation can’t track the AWS Application Auto Scaling resources.

In this post, we show you how to use a reusable CDK construct with AWS CloudFormation custom resources to orchestrate deregister and register auto scaling automatically during endpoint updates. You can update your endpoint configuration and auto scaling parameters in a single deployment without manual intervention.

Why this problem occurs

When you deploy a SageMaker AI endpoint with native CloudFormation auto scaling resources, then change the endpoint configuration and redeploy, several failure modes emerge. The specific failure depends on what you change and how you work around the issue.

Changing the endpoint configuration with auto scaling registered

CloudFormation tries to update the endpoint while the scalable target is still registered. SageMaker AI rejects the update with the following error:

SageMaker AI blocks the endpoint update before CloudFormation reaches the auto scaling resources.

Manually deregistering auto scaling, then changing only the endpoint configuration

If you deregister the scalable target through the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) and redeploy with only an endpoint configuration change, the deployment succeeds. However, CloudFormation doesn’t register auto scaling even though it is in the CloudFormation template. Because the auto scaling parameters in the CloudFormation template haven’t changed, CloudFormation doesn’t register the scalable target or re-apply the scaling policy. The endpoint is now running without auto scaling, and there is no error to indicate anything went wrong.

Manually deregistering auto scaling, then changing auto scaling parameters

If you deregister the scalable target through the AWS CLI and redeploy with auto scaling parameter changes, CloudFormation tries to update the ScalableTarget resource that no longer exists:

This failure is notable because the rollback also fails (UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED), leaving the stack in a broken state that requires manual intervention in the CloudFormation console to recover.

Solution overview

You can use this CDK construct to replace the native 

AWS::ApplicationAutoScaling::ScalableTarget
and 
AWS::ApplicationAutoScaling::ScalingPolicy
CloudFormation resources with three custom resources. These custom resources deregister and register auto scaling around the endpoint update with explicit dependency ordering, enforced by 
node.add_dependency
calls in CDK. The full sequence is:
  • Deregister (custom resource): Removes the scalable target before the endpoint update begins. On first deploy, no scalable target exists yet, so the handler handles the error gracefully and continues.
  • Endpoint update (CDK-managed): CDK updates the endpoint resource normally, swapping to the new endpoint configuration.
  • Register Scalable Target (custom resource): Waits for the endpoint to reach 
    InService
    status, then registers the scalable target.
  • Attach Scaling Policy (custom resource): Waits for the scalable target to be queryable, then applies the target tracking policy.

Register Scalable Target and Attach Scaling Policy use the CDK provider’s asynchronous completion pattern. Each custom resource has an 

on_event
handler that returns immediately and an 
is_complete
handler. The provider’s waiter re-invokes the 
is_complete
handler on an interval (every 30 seconds) until its readiness check passes. The provider’s 
total_timeout
(1 hour for Register Scalable Target, 15 minutes for Attach Scaling Policy) bounds the wait, so it isn’t limited by the timeout of any single Lambda invocation.

A 

ConfigHash
property on each custom resource forces CloudFormation to re-invoke the Lambda functions whenever a configuration value changes. The endpoint configuration and auto scaling parameters are defined together because a single 
ConfigHash
drives the auto scaling orchestration.

While the construct defines three custom resources, the deployed stack contains more than three Lambda functions. Each custom resource is backed by a CDK 

cr.Provider
, and the provider framework generates its own helper Lambda functions. A synchronous provider (Deregister) adds one framework function. An asynchronous provider (Register Scalable Target and Attach Scaling Policy) adds three (
onEvent
, 
isComplete
, and 
onTimeout
) plus an AWS Step Functions state machine that drives the waiter. As a result, the deployed stack contains three custom resources, two Step Functions state machines, and twelve Lambda functions. Five of the resources hold the construct’s own handler code (one for Deregister, and an 
on_event
and 
is_complete
pair for each asynchronous resource), with the remaining seven generated by the provider framework. You don’t write or maintain the framework-generated functions, but they are present in the stack and worth accounting for when you review the deployed resources.

Walkthrough

In this walkthrough, you deploy a SageMaker AI endpoint with auto scaling using the provided example stack, then verify that configuration updates work correctly.

The walkthrough includes the following steps:

  • Clone the repository and install dependencies.
  • Configure your endpoint and auto scaling settings.
  • Deploy and verify.
  • Test an update.

The source code is available in the linked GitHub repository.

Prerequisites

For this walkthrough, you need the following:

  • An AWS account with permissions for Amazon SageMaker AI, AWS Lambda, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), Application Auto Scaling, and Amazon CloudWatch.
  • AWS CDK v2 installed.
  • Python 3.12 or later.
  • uv for Python dependency management.
  • A SageMaker AI model artifact in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and a container image in Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR), or a SageMaker AI built-in algorithm container.

Clone the repository and install dependencies

  • Clone the repository:
  • Install dependencies:

Configure your endpoint and auto scaling settings

The endpoint and auto scaling settings are defined together in config/

config.yaml
because a single 
config_hash
drives the auto scaling orchestration. A change to either section triggers the full sequence.

Edit config/

config.yaml
with your values:

The endpoint parameters map to the SageMaker AI 

CreateModel
and 
CreateEndpointConfig
APIs. The auto scaling parameters map to the Application Auto Scaling 
RegisterScalableTarget
and 
PutScalingPolicy
APIs.

Deploy and verify

  • Bootstrap your AWS environment if you haven’t already:
  • Deploy the stack:

CloudFormation creates the SageMaker AI model, endpoint configuration, and endpoint, then runs the three custom resources in sequence to register auto scaling.

  • Verify that the deployment registered the scalable target:
  • Verify that the deployment applied the scaling policy:

Test an update

Change a value in config/

config.yaml
, for example, update the instance type from 
ml.m5.large
to 
ml.m5.xlarge
, and redeploy:

After the deployment completes, verify that auto scaling is still registered and has the updated values:

Integrating with an existing stack

Use the example stack if you’re starting fresh or want a reference implementation. Use the construct directly if you already have a CDK stack with SageMaker AI resources.

To integrate with an existing stack, copy the 

sagemaker_autoscaling/constructs/
directory into your project and add the construct alongside your endpoint resources:

How the construct works

This section walks through the key implementation details of 

SagemakerAutoscalingConstruct
.

Deregister

The Deregister custom resource calls 

deregister_scalable_target
before the endpoint update. It handles 
ObjectNotFoundException
for first deployments where no scalable target exists:

The dependency is established in CDK:

Register Scalable Target

Even though CloudFormation treats the endpoint resource as complete once the update is accepted, the scalable target can only be registered after the endpoint reaches 

InService
. Rather than block a single Lambda invocation on that wait, Register Scalable Target uses the provider’s asynchronous completion pattern. The 
on_event
handler returns immediately, and the provider’s waiter re-invokes the 
is_complete
handler on 
query_interval
until the endpoint is 
InService
. The provider’s 
total_timeout
(1 hour) bounds the wait, not the timeout of any single Lambda invocation:

On stack deletion, the 

on_event
handler deregisters the scalable target to clean up.

Attach Scaling Policy

There is a brief window after 

RegisterScalableTarget
returns where the target isn’t yet queryable. Attach Scaling Policy uses the same asynchronous completion pattern: the 
on_event
handler returns immediately, and the 
is_complete
handler reports completion only once the scalable target is queryable, at which point it applies the policy. The provider’s 
total_timeout
(15 minutes) bounds the wait:

On stack deletion, the 

on_event
handler deletes the scaling policy to clean up.

Cleaning up

To avoid incurring future charges, delete the resources:

This removes the SageMaker AI endpoint, endpoint configuration, model, Lambda functions, IAM roles, Amazon CloudWatch alarms created by the target tracking scaling policy, and deregisters the scalable target.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed you how to use a reusable CDK construct to deregister and register auto scaling automatically to orchestrate SageMaker AI endpoint updates. The construct uses three CloudFormation custom resources with explicit dependency ordering and a 

ConfigHash
property to keep auto scaling intact across deployments.

To get started, clone the 

sample-sagemaker-endpoint-autoscaling
repository and follow the setup instructions. The repository includes an example stack you can deploy directly, or you can integrate the construct into your existing CDK stack.

For more information about Application Auto Scaling for SageMaker AI, see Automatically scale Amazon SageMaker AI models. For more information about CloudFormation custom resources, see Custom resources in the AWS CloudFormation User Guide.

entries.title: Visualize points and routes with GeoJSON in Amazon Quick Sight layer maps
entries.summary: Amazon Quick Sight layer maps now support Point and LineString geometry from the same GeoJSON workflow, so you can plot store locations and the routes between them. This post covers the dataset and GeoJSON structure layer maps require, when to choose points or lines, and techniques for viewport control, layering geometries, and dynamic GeoJSON updates.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Visualize points and routes with GeoJSON in Amazon Quick Sight layer maps

With Amazon Quick Sight layer maps, you can now plot points and routes, like store locations across a city or flights leaving an airport. Geospatial maps help businesses spot patterns that are tied to location, like how a region is performing or where customers are concentrated. Amazon Quick Sight supports this with multiple map types, including point maps, filled maps, and layer maps. When layer maps first launched, you could upload a GeoJSON file to draw custom shape layers, such as sales territories or districts, and join those shapes to a dataset. That handled regions and boundaries well, but it didn’t cover the individual locations inside them or the routes running between them.

Layer maps now support two more geometry types from the same GeoJSON workflow: Point and LineString. Points mark specific locations, such as individual store or facility sites. A LineString traces the route between locations, like a delivery path or a flight between airports.

Amazon Quick Sight, the business intelligence (BI) capability of Amazon Quick, is a unified BI service. It delivers modern interactive dashboards, natural language querying, pixel-perfect reports, machine learning (ML) insights, and embedded analytics at scale. Amazon Quick brings together AI agents for business insights, research, and automation in one integrated experience, helping you work smarter and faster while maintaining security and access policies.

In this post, we walk through the dataset and GeoJSON structure that layer maps require. We also explain how points and lines work in a layer map visual and when to choose each. Finally, we cover advanced techniques for controlling the viewport, layering geometries, and updating GeoJSON files programmatically.

Dataset structure considerations

A layer map gets its shapes from a GeoJSON file and its metrics from a Quick Sight dataset, and a shared key joins the two. How you structure each one determines what the map can show. This section covers what you need before you start and how a GeoJSON file is organized.

Prerequisites

The following are the prerequisites that you need before creating a layer map in Quick Sight:

  • A GeoJSON file describing your geometry.
  • A Quick Sight dataset holding the metrics and dimensions.
  • A join key shared between the Quick Sight dataset and the GeoJSON file.
  • The GeoJSON file must be saved in .geojson format, with a maximum supported file size of 100 MB.

Structure of the GeoJSON file

GeoJSON is a JSON-based format for describing geographic features such as points and lines.

The structure of the file is as follows:

  • FeatureCollection is the whole file. It has a type of FeatureCollection and a features array.
  • Feature is a single map element. It carries a geometry (the shape) and a properties object, which holds the join key.
  • geometry has a type (Point, LineString, or Polygon) and its coordinates. The coordinates hold a single [longitude, latitude] position for a Point, and an ordered list of positions for a LineString.

Configuring the Quick Sight dataset and its GeoJSON

In Quick Sight, when you configure a layer in a layer map visual, there are two primary settings to consider. The first is the Geometry type to visualize, which sets which geometry from the GeoJSON file renders: Points, Lines, or Polygons. A layer renders one geometry type at a time, so when a file mixes types like the preceding example, only Features of the selected type appear on the map. The second is matching the Shape file key field to the Dataset key field, which links each Feature in the GeoJSON to a row in your Quick Sight dataset. The field names don’t need to be identical, but the values do. The following two examples show this end to end, first a LineString layer and then a Point layer.

Example: LineString layer

Consider example data showing a flight from JFK to a destination city like Los Angeles. The GeoJSON structure for a single datapoint is configured as follows:

The corresponding row in the Quick Sight dataset contains the following information:

The route_id field is used to join the Quick Sight dataset with the GeoJSON file. The GeoJSON holds one such feature per route, and the dataset one row per route. The Geometry type to visualize is set to Lines.

Example: Point layer

Consider example data showing a retail store location like Long Island City. The GeoJSON structure for a single datapoint is configured as follows:

The corresponding row in the Quick Sight dataset contains the following information:

The store_id field is used to join the Quick Sight dataset with the GeoJSON file. The GeoJSON holds one such feature per store, and the dataset one row per store. The Geometry type to visualize is set to Points.

Lines on layer map visuals

Layer map visuals now support LineString geometry, connecting an ordered list of coordinates into a single path. As covered in the data structure section, each route is one feature, and its coordinates are the ordered positions the map connects in sequence.

Use lines when the relationship between locations is what you want to show, such as flight paths, delivery routes, shipping lanes, or pipeline segments. The visual draws each path from the coordinates in your GeoJSON file rather than generating it from your data at load time. A field from your joined dataset can determine the line color encoding, so you can group routes by whatever that field represents. In addition to color, you can customize lines with width and opacity controls to adjust visual prominence and clarity on the map. The join key in the GeoJSON properties object ties each LineString to the dataset row behind its tooltip and color.

For example, an airport operations team might map the flights leaving New York (JFK) on a given day. The GeoJSON file holds one LineString per route, keyed by a route ID that joins to the dataset. Each line starts at JFK and ends at its destination, such as Los Angeles, Chicago, or Miami. The dataset supplies the origin, destination, and carrier that show up in the tooltip.

Points on layer map visuals

Amazon Quick Sight offers a native point map visual type that geocodes location names automatically and refreshes with your SPICE schedule or Direct Query connection. It supports dynamic point sizing, color encoding, and point styles such as cluster points and heatmap density gradients.
